transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I came in because... I had to do this physical for my insurance. Which is a whole hassle on its own, honestly. My company switched providers back in January and the new paperwork is just endless, they want to know every little thing. But anyway, the doctor doing that physical said my weight was too low. 

I think he's overreacting, honestly. To me, I just look lean from being on ladders and working long days. I mean, painting is really physical work. Just last week we were doing the exterior of this old Victorian place over in the Heights, and man, the scaffolding was an absolute nightmare to set up. The ground was all uneven from the rain we've been having, so we spent half the morning just leveling the base plates. You really can't mess around with safety when you're three stories up with a heavy paint sprayer. My buddy Dave actually fell off a ladder a few years ago and messed up his shoulder pretty bad, so I'm always super careful about the setup. 

But yeah, so that insurance doctor got all hung up on my weight and told me I needed to come see someone, even though I'm just working hard, you know?
Do you think your weight is normal for you?

Normal? Yeah, I mean, I think it is. I know my buddies on the crew and that insurance doctor are all worried about it, but I really feel like they're just overreacting. I mean, I'm still showing up to jobs every single day and getting all my work done, right? 

Actually, I'm usually the only one showing up on time lately. We hired this new kid, Tyler, a few weeks ago to help out. He’s supposed to be at the site by 6 AM to help prep and tape the windows. Taping is the most important part, honestly. If you use that cheap blue tape instead of the good green edge tape, the paint bleeds right through onto the glass, and then you're spending hours with a razor blade just scraping it off in the hot sun. It's the worst. And Tyler? He rolls in at 7:30 with an iced coffee, doesn't even apologize. It's just impossible to find good help right now, nobody wants to put in the hours. 

But yeah, anyway, I'm out there every day working circles around these younger guys, so I really don't get why everyone is making such a fuss about my size.
Do you feel like you have a normal appetite?

My appetite? I mean, I guess it's normal for me. Most days I just stick to coffee in the morning. Maybe I'll grab a protein bar between jobs if I remember, and then just a small dinner at night. Eating a big, full meal during the day just feels like it would totally slow me down, you know? You get that heavy feeling in your stomach and then you're supposed to climb back up a 40-foot extension ladder? No way. 

Speaking of ladders, I actually have to go pick up a new one this weekend. The locking mechanism on my old aluminum one is starting to stick. It's a Werner, usually they're pretty reliable, but I left it out in the rain a couple times last month when we were doing that big commercial job over on 4th Street. That job was a total nightmare, by the way. The general contractor kept changing the paint colors after we had already primed everything. We had to go back to Sherwin-Williams like three times to get different shades of gray. Who knew there were so many shades of gray? Repose Gray, Mindful Gray, Dorian Gray... it's ridiculous. And the guy at the paint counter, Mike, he's always so slow. You're standing there for twenty minutes just waiting for him to mix a five-gallon bucket. 

So yeah, I just keep it light during the day. Don't really have the time or the appetite for much else when I'm working.
Have you been trying to lose weight?

Trying to lose? I mean, not exactly trying to lose, but I definitely don't want to gain anything. Like, if the scale goes up even a tiny bit after a client dinner or if I eat something with bread, I get pretty tense. I always make sure to start cutting back the next day so the weight doesn't stick. 

Speaking of client dinners, they are just a massive headache anyway. I had to meet this guy, Mr. Henderson, a couple weeks ago at this fancy Italian place downtown to go over a bid for a huge interior job. The parking down there is an absolute joke. I had to wedge my work truck into this tiny underground garage like six blocks away. You know how wide those F-150s are, right? The turning radius is just garbage. I swear I was a quarter inch away from scraping the entire side of my truck bed against this concrete pillar. It had yellow paint scraped all over it, so clearly I wasn't the first guy to misjudge the corner. 

And then I finally get to the table and Henderson just talks my ear off about his golf swing for an hour before we even look at the contract. I don't even get golf, honestly. You're just walking around hitting a little ball into a hole, it's not a real workout. But yeah, if I end up eating that kind of heavy restaurant food with clients, I just make sure to cut way back the next day.
Are you afraid of gaining weight?

Well, like I was just saying, yeah... I guess afraid is the right word. If I see the scale go up even a tiny bit, like after one of those dinners or if I eat something with bread, I get really tense. I just have to start cutting back the very next day so it doesn't stick. 

Bread is just... it's so heavy. Actually, there's this artisanal bakery right next to the Victorian we're painting this week over on Elm Street. They start baking sourdough at like 4 AM, so by the time I'm out there setting up the scaffolding, the whole block just smells unbelievable. We're doing all the exterior trim on the house next door, and let me tell you, the owner picked this absolute nightmare of a color. It's this bright, mustard yellow. I tried to tell the guy, I said, "Look, buddy, this is gonna completely clash with your red brick," but he wouldn't listen. People just have zero eye for color these days. They see some trendy design on HGTV and think it's gonna work on a classic 1920s house. It’s ridiculous. Plus, yellow is notorious for terrible hide. I'm gonna have to put on three coats of the stuff just to get it to cover the old dark green paint. It's eating up my entire profit margin on labor alone. 

But yeah, anyway... I just get really anxious about the weight sticking if I eat stuff like that, so I make sure to fix it immediately the next day.
Does worrying about your weight affect your daily activities or relationships?

I mean, I'm still getting all my painting jobs done, you know? The work doesn't stop. But... I guess I do avoid some client meals now. And social plans with the guys. I just really don't want to deal with a situation where people start commenting on what I'm eating, or how I look, or why I'm not ordering a beer. 

Speaking of the guys, my buddy Dave, who works on my crew sometimes, he just got this new rescue dog. It's some kind of pitbull mix, I think. He brings it to the job sites sometimes, which is honestly a terrible idea. Last week we were doing an interior job, just some basic eggshell on the walls, and the dog gets loose in the house. It's running around, sliding on the drop cloths, knocking over my cut-in bucket... I swear, I almost had a heart attack. If that dog had tracked Navajo White paint all over this lady's original hardwood floors, I would have been paying for it for the next five years. Hardwood floors are so expensive to refinish now. You have to rent the big drum sander, and the edger, and the sandpaper alone costs a fortune. Plus the dust gets everywhere. You find dust in the air vents six months later. 

But yeah, I just try to avoid those meals and hangouts if I can. It's just easier than having people watch me eat.
Do you avoid certain foods because you're afraid of gaining weight?

Well, yeah, I definitely avoid certain things. I mean, most days I really just keep it to coffee, maybe I'll grab a protein bar between paint jobs if I really need to, and then just a small dinner. Eating a full, heavy meal just... it feels like it would totally slow me down, you know? 

And you really can't afford to slow down when you're doing exterior work, especially this time of year. The weather is so unpredictable right now. Like, yesterday, the forecast said zero percent chance of rain. Zero. So I get all the masking tape up, I lay out the plastic sheeting over the bushes—which, by the way, is a huge pain because this client has these massive, thorny rose bushes right up against the foundation. I don't know why people plant those things so close to the house, it's terrible for the siding. It traps all the moisture and rots the wood. Anyway, I get the sprayer primed, I'm halfway through the first coat on the south side of the house, and suddenly the sky just opens up. Just a complete downpour. I had to scramble to get everything covered so the fresh paint wouldn't wash right off onto the driveway. If it rains on wet latex paint, it creates this milky streak down the wall and you basically have to sand it all down and start completely over once it dries. It's a total nightmare. 

But yeah, anyway, I just stick to coffee and a protein bar during the day so I don't feel weighed down or sluggish while I'm working.
Are there any activities you've stopped doing because of your concerns about weight?

Not really... I mean, I'm still doing all my normal stuff. Still working, still going to the gym. I haven't really stopped doing anything, I don't think. 

Speaking of the gym, though, they just installed these new overhead lights in the weight room, and they are blinding. I don't know who does the electrical contracting for that place, but they used these cool-toned LEDs, like 5000 Kelvin at least. It feels like you're in a hospital operating room, not a place to work out. I was trying to tell the manager, I said, "You need a warmer color temperature, maybe 3000K, or at least put them on a dimmer switch." Because when you're laying on the bench press looking straight up, it's just searing your retinas. Plus, that harsh blue light is terrible for the paint on the walls in there. It completely washes out the color. They have this nice slate gray on the walls, but under those lights, it just looks like a dirty, institutional blue. It's amazing how lighting can completely change the way a paint color reads in a room. You can have a beautiful warm beige, and if you put the wrong bulb in the fixture, suddenly it looks like a muddy green. 

But no, to answer your question, I haven't really quit any activities or anything like that. Just keeping busy.
Do you feel like your concerns about weight are affecting your overall happiness or well-being?

I don't know if it's affecting my happiness, really. I mean, I'm just living my life, doing my job. I don't feel unhappy, per se. Just... busy, I guess. 

Speaking of being busy, I've got this huge exterior job coming up next week on this old Victorian house downtown. The amount of prep work on those old places is just insane. You can't just slap a coat of paint on and call it a day. You've got to scrape all the peeling paint, and since it was built in, like, 1910, you have to be super careful about lead paint. You have to put down the heavy-duty plastic, wear the respirator, use the special HEPA vacs... it's a whole process. And the trim work on these Victorians, the "gingerbread" stuff? It takes forever. You're up on a forty-foot extension ladder with a tiny little sash brush, just trying to get into all these little crevices. My shoulders are already aching just thinking about it. I usually have to ice my rotator cuff every night when I'm doing a Victorian. But they do look incredible when they're finished. There's nothing like seeing an old house brought back to life with a fresh color scheme. The client wants to do a historic palette—like a deep olive green for the body, cream trim, and maybe a dark burgundy for the accents. It's going to pop. 

But yeah, happiness-wise... I think I'm doing alright. Just, you know, focused on the work.
Do you think your concerns about weight are impacting your ability to enjoy your work or daily activities?

Well, I'm still getting all my painting jobs done, so it's not really impacting my work itself. But I guess... I do avoid some client meals or, like, social plans with friends lately. I just really don't want the situation to turn into people commenting on what I eat or how I look, you know? It's just easier to bow out. 

Especially with clients, they always want to feed you when you're working inside their house. Like this one lady last month, I was painting her dining room and kitchen—which, by the way, painting kitchens is a total nightmare if the homeowner doesn't clean properly. People don't realize how much cooking grease aerosolizes and settles onto the walls and ceiling. If you don't scrub the walls down with TSP—trisodium phosphate—before you even think about putting up painter's tape, your new paint is just going to bead up and peel right off in sheets. You absolutely cannot just paint over cooking grease. 

Anyway, she kept trying to get me to sit down and eat this big heavy lunch with her and her husband, and I just had to keep making excuses and staying out in the garage. And speaking of her dining room, she chose this incredibly dark navy blue. Beautiful color, but dark colors like that have virtually no hide. You have to use a tinted primer, usually a dark gray, and even then, you're looking at three coats minimum to get a solid, even finish without flashing. And if you don't keep a wet edge while you're rolling, you will see every single roller mark when the afternoon light hits it from the window. It took me three days just to do that one room because of the dry time between coats. 

But yeah, I just try to avoid eating with people so I don't have to deal with the comments. It just makes things simpler.
Do you ever feel like your concerns about weight are controlling your life?

Controlling my life? No, I wouldn't go that far. I mean, I'm the one making my own choices. I've always liked being in control of things, honestly. You kind of have to be in my line of work. 

If you aren't in complete control of a job site, everything just falls apart. Especially when you're doing high-end finishes, like spraying kitchen cabinets. You have to have absolute control over the environment. You have to build a complete containment zone with zip poles and thick plastic sheeting, or else that fine overspray from the HVLP gun gets everywhere. And I mean everywhere. It will literally get sucked into the cold air return and travel through the HVAC system, and suddenly the homeowner's upstairs bedrooms are covered in a fine layer of white lacquer dust. It's a nightmare. 

And you have to control the humidity and temperature in the room, too. If it's too humid when you spray lacquer, it does this thing called blushing. It gets this cloudy, milky look trapped right under the surface because moisture got caught in the finish while the solvents were flashing off. You can't just wipe it away once it happens, either. You have to get out the orbital sander, take it all the way back down to bare wood, and start completely over. It's a massive waste of time and materials. So you have to be the one dictating exactly how the space is set up. 

But, uh... what was the question? Oh, right, controlling my life. No, I don't feel like anything is controlling me. I just have my routines and I stick to them.
Are there specific situations or activities where you feel like your weight concerns are holding you back?

Like I was mentioning earlier, it's really just the social stuff. Work-wise, nothing is holding me back. I'm still getting all my painting jobs done, hitting all my deadlines. But I guess it's like what I said before about the client meals—I just avoid social plans with friends now, too. I just don't want to go and have the whole situation turn into people commenting on what I'm eating, or making remarks about how I look. It's exhausting. 

Like, my buddy Dave invited me to a cookout this past weekend, and I just made up an excuse not to go. Dave actually subcontracts for me sometimes when I get backed up. We did this massive cedar deck restoration together last August, and man, decks are the absolute worst if the previous homeowner didn't maintain them right. People always think you can just blast it with a pressure washer and slap on some cheap sealer, but that's a huge mistake. If there's an old acrylic stain on there, you have to use a chemical stripper, and it is nasty stuff. You have to wear these heavy chemical-resistant gloves and scrub it into the grain with a stiff bristle brush. 

And the step everyone skips—you have to neutralize the wood afterward with oxalic acid. Wood brightener. If you don't use the brightener, the pH balance of the wood is totally out of whack from the stripper, and your new stain will look completely blotchy and probably fail within a year. Plus, you have to check the boards with a moisture meter and make sure it's reading below fifteen percent before you can even think about applying a penetrating oil stain. We actually had to pack up and wait three extra days on that job because it rained and the wood swelled up. 

But anyway, yeah. Dave's cookout. I just skipped it. I'd rather just stay home than deal with the comments, you know? It's just easier to avoid it altogether.
Do you think your concerns about weight are interfering with your ability to enjoy your daily life?

I feel like I'm a bit of a broken record here, but yeah, it's basically what I was saying before. My daily life is mostly work, and I'm still getting all my painting jobs done on time, so that part is fine. It's just... I avoid the client meals and the social plans because I really, really don't want to deal with people commenting on what I'm eating or how I look. It just ruins the enjoyment of the day, you know? 

Like, if I'm working on a historic home—which I do a lot of in the older neighborhoods downtown—the homeowners always want to come out and offer you sandwiches or sit on the porch with you. And those old houses, man, you have to be so incredibly careful. If the house was built before 1978, you're almost definitely dealing with lead paint. You can't just go out there and scrape it dry like a normal house. You have to follow strict EPA RRP rules—Renovation, Repair, and Painting. You have to lay down heavy six-mil plastic extending at least ten feet out from the foundation, tape it to the house, put up caution signs, and you have to wet-scrape everything so the lead dust doesn't become airborne or get into the soil. 

If the EPA or OSHA catches you dry-scraping lead paint, the fines are absolutely astronomical. We're talking tens of thousands of dollars per violation. Plus, you have to wear a P100 half-mask respirator the entire time, and let me tell you, it gets so incredibly hot breathing inside that heavy rubber mask in the middle of July. You're sweating buckets, your safety glasses are fogging up. You have to wear a disposable Tyvek suit, too. 

So the absolute last thing I want to do is go through the whole decontamination process, take all my PPE off, just to sit on the porch and have a homeowner watch me eat and make little remarks about my portion sizes or my weight. So yeah, I just tell them I eat in my truck or that I have a strict schedule to keep. It just saves me the headache.
Have you noticed any changes in your relationships with friends or family due to your concerns about weight?

I know I keep saying the exact same thing, but it really just comes down to what I mentioned before. Work is totally fine, I'm still getting all my painting jobs done without a hitch. But with friends and family... yeah, things have definitely changed because I just avoid social plans now. 

Like my sister, she wanted me to come over for dinner last week and also look at this patch job she did on her hallway wall. And man, people think drywall repair is so easy, like you just buy a little pink tub of spackle and smear it on with a putty knife. But you can't do that on a big hole. You have to cut the drywall out square, put in wood backing strips, and use actual joint tape. I always prefer paper tape over the fiberglass mesh, because the mesh can crack on you if you don't use a hot mud—like a setting-type compound that cures chemically instead of just drying out. 

And then the most important part is you have to feather it out. You need a six-inch taping knife to bed the tape, then a ten-inch for the fill coat, and then a twelve-inch knife to really blend it into the rest of the wall. If you don't feather it wide enough, the second you put a coat of eggshell or satin paint on there and the hall light hits it, you're gonna see this massive, ugly hump in the wall. It drives me crazy when people just glob premixed joint compound on there and think they can sand it flat with a little sponge. You need a pole sander, and you have to shine a raking light across the wall to actually check your work before you even think about priming it. 

But anyway, yeah, she wanted to do this whole big family dinner thing while I looked at her wall, and I just made up an excuse not to go. I just avoid those situations, same as the client meals. I just do not want the situation to turn into people sitting around a table commenting on what I eat or how I look. It’s just easier to stay away.
Do you think you would feel better about yourself if you gained a little weight?

Gained a little weight? No. No, man, absolutely not. If the scale goes up even a little bit, like if I do end up at a client dinner or eat something with bread, I get incredibly tense. 

Actually, a lot of those client dinners happen right in the middle of kitchen remodels. I just quoted a massive kitchen job yesterday. The homeowners want me to paint their old nineties honey oak cabinets white. And everybody watches those DIY shows and thinks you can just slap some latex paint over varnished oak with a foam roller. It's ridiculous. Oak has deep open grain, and the tannin bleed will come right through water-based paint in a week, turning it yellow. You have to scrub years of cooking grease off with TSP, sand every single contour of those doors, and then you have to spray a shellac-based primer. 

And let me tell you, spraying shellac is a completely different beast. You need an airless sprayer with a fine finish tip—like a 310 or 312—and because shellac dries so fast, if you stop for even five minutes, the tip clogs solid. Plus, the masking... oh man. It takes three full days just to mask a kitchen. You have to wrap the entire room in plastic, cover the floors in heavy Ram Board, tape off all the appliances... because if atomized shellac overspray lands on a custom granite countertop, you are basically buying them a new kitchen. You have to clean the whole rig out with ammonia or denatured alcohol afterward, too, you can't just run water or paint thinner through it. 

But, uh... anyway. What were we talking about? Oh, right. Gaining weight. Yeah, no, if I see that scale move up at all after eating something heavy, I just start cutting back the next day so it doesn't stick. I definitely wouldn't feel better about myself if I gained.
Do you ever find yourself thinking about your weight when you're not trying to?

Yeah, it sneaks up on me a lot. Like... if I catch myself in a mirror, or especially in photos next to one of my murals. 

I do a lot of large-scale commercial murals for businesses around town, mostly on the sides of old buildings. And man, those exterior brick jobs are exhausting. People don't realize you can't just slap regular exterior latex on raw brick. The alkalinity in the masonry will literally burn the tint right out of the paint in six months. You have to pressure wash it first, let it dry completely, and then back-roll a heavy coat of masonry primer—something like Loxon—into every single mortar joint. You go through roller covers like crazy because the brick just shreds them. A three-quarter-inch nap is the bare minimum, and even then you're constantly jamming the brush in there to fill the pinholes. 

And getting the proportions right on a two-story wall is a whole other nightmare. I usually have to rent a tow-behind boom lift, wait until it's pitch black outside, and shine a high-lumen projector from across the street just to trace the outline. If you mess up the grid or the angle of the projector is off by even a few degrees, the whole image gets warped. 

So you put all this blood, sweat, and tears into it for weeks... and then the business owner comes out and wants to take a picture of you standing next to the finished piece for their social media. And honestly? When I look at those photos, or if I just catch my reflection in the storefront glass while I'm loading the lift back onto the trailer, I'm not even looking at the artwork I just spent weeks on. I basically judge the whole day by whether my stomach and face look sharp enough in that moment. It just completely takes over my head, even when I'm supposed to be celebrating a finished job.
Do you ever find it difficult to stop thinking about your weight, even when you're trying to focus on something else?

Yeah, I mean, it's pretty much what I just said, honestly. It's really hard to turn it off. Like I said about the murals, I'll catch myself in a mirror or in those photos next to a finished piece, and I'll literally judge my entire day based on whether my stomach and face look sharp enough. It completely hijacks my brain. 

And it's really frustrating because those commercial jobs take so much out of you. Especially if you're dealing with a textured surface like stucco. Stucco is even worse than brick. You can't roll it. You have to spray it, and if it's an old building, the stucco is usually chalky, so you have to use a masonry conditioner first to bind the surface. Otherwise, the paint just peels off in big sheets a year later. 

And the masking for exterior spray jobs is a nightmare. You have to use special tape that sticks to masonry but won't pull the paint off the window frames, and you have to drape plastic over everything—cars, landscaping, the sidewalk. If the wind picks up even a little bit, overspray can drift for blocks. I had a buddy who sprayed a building on a slightly breezy day, and he ended up having to pay to detail like fifteen cars parked down the street because they all had tiny specks of gray paint on them. You have to use a low-pressure spray tip, keep the gun exactly twelve inches from the wall, and overlap your passes by fifty percent. If you don't, you get these vertical stripes where the paint is thicker. We call it "tiger striping." It looks terrible. 

But, uh... yeah. Even when I'm dealing with all that stress, the wind, the overspray, the boom lift... if I see my reflection in a window I'm taping off, the whole job just fades into the background, and all I can think about is my stomach. It's really hard to stop it.
Do you find yourself thinking about your weight even when you're not actively trying to think about it or worry about it?

I mean... yeah, it happens all the time. Like I was saying before, it just kind of pops into my head whether I want it to or not. If I'm walking past a storefront or if a client tags me in a photo next to a mural I just finished, I'm not looking at the art. I'll literally judge my entire day based on whether my stomach and face look sharp enough in that split second. 

And man, storefront glass is the worst because you're usually dealing with aluminum mullions. People always ask me to paint those aluminum window frames, and they think you can just hit it with some spray paint. You absolutely cannot. Aluminum oxidizes, so if you don't use a self-etching primer or an epoxy primer, whatever you put on top is going to peel off in sheets the second the sun hits it. You have to scuff the metal with a red Scotch-Brite pad, wipe it down with a strong solvent—like acetone or MEK—and then you have to spray the primer while the metal is still completely clean. If you wait even a day, a microscopic layer of oxidation forms, and the paint won't bite. 

And masking around commercial glass? It takes forever. You can't just use regular blue tape because the UV rays from the sun will bake the adhesive onto the glass in like two hours. You have to use a special green or orange UV-resistant tape, and even then, you don't want to leave it on there for more than a few days. If you do, you'll be out there with a razor scraper and Goof Off for hours, just trying to get the sticky residue off. I actually had a guy working for me once who left regular masking tape on a south-facing window for a week. I had to pay him for a full eight-hour day just to scrape tape off glass. It was a total nightmare. 

But, um... yeah. I definitely think about it when I'm not trying to. It just sneaks up on me, especially when I see those photos or catch my reflection.
Do you think about your weight first thing in the morning?

Yeah, I do. It's usually the first thing that hits me when I wake up. I'll get out of bed, and before I even make coffee, I'm already thinking about it. Like I was saying, it's that same feeling I get when I catch myself in a mirror or look at those photos next to my murals. I basically judge my whole day, right from the start, based on whether my stomach and face look sharp enough. 

And mornings are tough anyway because you have to get an early start if you're doing exterior work in the summer. You really want to be on the job site by 6:00 AM, right when the sun comes up, because you have to chase the shade. If you try to paint a wall that's in direct sunlight, the surface temperature of the brick or the metal can easily hit 140 degrees. When the wall is that hot, the paint flashes—it dries way too fast. You can't even keep a wet edge, and you end up with lap marks everywhere. Plus, the water evaporates out of the latex before the acrylic resins have time to coalesce and form a proper film, so the paint just fails prematurely. 

So you have to plan your whole day around the sun. You start on the west side of the building in the morning, and by noon, you've moved to the east side. It's a logistical headache, especially if you have to move a boom lift around tight corners or navigate around parked cars. I had this one job painting a massive warehouse, and the property manager refused to block off the parking spaces. I was trying to maneuver a 60-foot articulated boom lift between these expensive cars, terrified I was going to drop a roller or drip paint on a Mercedes. 

But yeah... it's right there in the morning. Even before I'm thinking about the sun or the boom lift, I'm already judging how my stomach looks.
Do you think about your weight at times when it doesn't seem relevant to what you're doing?

Yeah, definitely. I know I sound like a broken record here, but it's exactly what I've been saying about catching myself in a mirror or looking at those photos next to my murals. It has absolutely nothing to do with the job I'm working on, but I'll still judge my whole day by whether my stomach and face look sharp enough in that moment. 

Like, I could be right in the middle of a massive interior job. You know, when a client wants to go from a dark navy blue or a crimson red to a stark white? People think paint is just magic. It's really not. If you don't use a high-hide primer—usually something tinted slightly gray, actually, because gray covers dark colors way better than white does—you're going to be putting on four coats of expensive topcoat. And even then, the dark color will flash through under certain lighting. And you have to use a 3/8-inch nap microfiber roller, because if you use a half-inch, it leaves way too much stipple, and the wall ends up looking like an orange peel. 

And don't even get me started on drywall dust. If the drywall guys didn't wipe down the walls with a damp sponge after sanding the mud, your primer is just going to stick to the dust, not the paper. I've seen whole strips of paint just peel right off the wall and wrap around the roller because of drywall dust. You have to use a PVA primer to seal the porous mud first, otherwise the finish coat flashes and looks completely dead and uneven in the spots where the joints are. 

But... yeah. I could be dealing with all that, stressing over whether the red is bleeding through the primer, and if I catch my reflection in a glossy door frame I just painted... the job doesn't matter anymore. All the technical stuff just drops out of my head, and it's straight back to stressing over my stomach.

doctor.intent: identify chief complaint
doctor.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

target_item.name: Low_Weight
target_item.manifestation: I came in because the doctor doing my insurance physical said my weight was too low, though to me I just look lean from being on ladders and working long days.
target_item.reason: This is the first reply of the consultation, so I must return the chief complaint symptom code (S044) regardless of the doctor's opening question.

patient.answer:
Well, I came in because... I had to do this physical for my insurance. Which is a whole hassle on its own, honestly. My company switched providers back in January and the new paperwork is just endless, they want to know every little thing. But anyway, the doctor doing that physical said my weight was too low.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I mean, it's pretty much what I just said, honestly. It's really hard to turn it off. Like I said about the murals, I'll catch myself in a mirror or in those photos next to a finished piece, and I'll literally judge my entire day based on whether my stomach and face look sharp enough. It completely hijacks my brain. 

And it's really frustrating because those commercial jobs take so much out of you. Especially if you're dealing with a textured surface like stucco. Stucco is even worse than brick. You can't roll it. You have to spray it, and if it's an old building, the stucco is usually chalky, so you have to use a masonry conditioner first to bind the surface. Otherwise, the paint just peels off in big sheets a year later. 

And the masking for exterior spray jobs is a nightmare. You have to use special tape that sticks to masonry but won't pull the paint off the window frames, and you have to drape plastic over everything—cars, landscaping, the sidewalk. If the wind picks up even a little bit, overspray can drift for blocks. I had a buddy who sprayed a building on a slightly breezy day, and he ended up having to pay to detail like fifteen cars parked down the street because they all had tiny specks of gray paint on them. You have to use a low-pressure spray tip, keep the gun exactly twelve inches from the wall, and overlap your passes by fifty percent. If you don't, you get these vertical stripes where the paint is thicker. We call it "tiger striping." It looks terrible. 

But, uh... yeah. Even when I'm dealing with all that stress, the wind, the overspray, the boom lift... if I see my reflection in a window I'm taping off, the whole job just fades into the background, and all I can think about is my stomach. It's really hard to stop it.

doctor.intent: determine if patient's weight concerns are an obsessive thought pattern
doctor.question: Do you find yourself thinking about your weight even when you're not actively trying to think about it or worry about it?

target_item.name: Body_Image_Weight_Shape_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: When I catch myself in a mirror or in photos next to one of my murals, I judge the whole day by whether my stomach and face look sharp enough.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about intrusive thoughts or preoccupation with weight, which relates to the undue influence of body weight or shape on the patient's self-evaluation.

patient.answer:
I mean... yeah, it happens all the time. Like I was saying before, it just kind of pops into my head whether I want it to or not. If I'm walking past a storefront or if a client tags me in a photo next to a mural I just finished, I'm not looking at the art. I'll literally judge my entire day based on whether my stomach and face look sharp enough in that split second. 

And man, storefront glass is the worst because you're usually dealing with aluminum mullions. People always ask me to paint those aluminum window frames, and they think you can just hit it with some spray paint. You absolutely cannot. Aluminum oxidizes, so if you don't use a self-etching primer or an epoxy primer, whatever you put on top is going to peel off in sheets the second the sun hits it. You have to scuff the metal with a red Scotch-Brite pad, wipe it down with a strong solvent—like acetone or MEK—and then you have to spray the primer while the metal is still completely clean. If you wait even a day, a microscopic layer of oxidation forms, and the paint won't bite. 

And masking around commercial glass? It takes forever. You can't just use regular blue tape because the UV rays from the sun will bake the adhesive onto the glass in like two hours. You have to use a special green or orange UV-resistant tape, and even then, you don't want to leave it on there for more than a few days. If you do, you'll be out there with a razor scraper and Goof Off for hours, just trying to get the sticky residue off. I actually had a guy working for me once who left regular masking tape on a south-facing window for a week. I had to pay him for a full eight-hour day just to scrape tape off glass. It was a total nightmare. 

But, um... yeah. I definitely think about it when I'm not trying to. It just sneaks up on me, especially when I see those photos or catch my reflection.

doctor.intent: Determine if patient's weight concerns are an obsessive thought pattern
doctor.question: Do you think about your weight first thing in the morning?

target_item.name: Body_Image_Weight_Shape_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: When I catch myself in a mirror or in photos next to one of my murals, I judge the whole day by whether my stomach and face look sharp enough.
target_item.reason: The doctor is continuing to ask about how often and when I think about my weight, which relates to the undue influence of body weight and shape on my self-evaluation.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I do. It's usually the first thing that hits me when I wake up. I'll get out of bed, and before I even make coffee, I'm already thinking about it. Like I was saying, it's that same feeling I get when I catch myself in a mirror or look at those photos next to my murals. I basically judge my whole day, right from the start, based on whether my stomach and face look sharp enough. 

And mornings are tough anyway because you have to get an early start if you're doing exterior work in the summer. You really want to be on the job site by 6:00 AM, right when the sun comes up, because you have to chase the shade. If you try to paint a wall that's in direct sunlight, the surface temperature of the brick or the metal can easily hit 140 degrees. When the wall is that hot, the paint flashes—it dries way too fast. You can't even keep a wet edge, and you end up with lap marks everywhere. Plus, the water evaporates out of the latex before the acrylic resins have time to coalesce and form a proper film, so the paint just fails prematurely. 

So you have to plan your whole day around the sun. You start on the west side of the building in the morning, and by noon, you've moved to the east side. It's a logistical headache, especially if you have to move a boom lift around tight corners or navigate around parked cars. I had this one job painting a massive warehouse, and the property manager refused to block off the parking spaces. I was trying to maneuver a 60-foot articulated boom lift between these expensive cars, terrified I was going to drop a roller or drip paint on a Mercedes. 

But yeah... it's right there in the morning. Even before I'm thinking about the sun or the boom lift, I'm already judging how my stomach looks.

doctor.intent: determine if patient's weight concerns are an obsessive thought
doctor.question: Do you think about your weight at times when it doesn't seem relevant to what you're doing?

target_item.name: Body_Image_Weight_Shape_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: When I catch myself in a mirror or in photos next to one of my murals, I judge the whole day by whether my stomach and face look sharp enough.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question about thinking of weight at irrelevant times continues to assess the extent and intrusiveness of the patient's preoccupation with their body weight and shape, which aligns with the undue influence of weight/shape on self-evaluation.

patient.answer:
Yeah, definitely. I know I sound like a broken record here, but it's exactly what I've been saying about catching myself in a mirror or looking at those photos next to my murals. It has absolutely nothing to do with the job I'm working on, but I'll still judge my whole day by whether my stomach and face look sharp enough in that moment. 

Like, I could be right in the middle of a massive interior job. You know, when a client wants to go from a dark navy blue or a crimson red to a stark white? People think paint is just magic. It's really not. If you don't use a high-hide primer—usually something tinted slightly gray, actually, because gray covers dark colors way better than white does—you're going to be putting on four coats of expensive topcoat. And even then, the dark color will flash through under certain lighting. And you have to use a 3/8-inch nap microfiber roller, because if you use a half-inch, it leaves way too much stipple, and the wall ends up looking like an orange peel. 

And don't even get me started on drywall dust. If the drywall guys didn't wipe down the walls with a damp sponge after sanding the mud, your primer is just going to stick to the dust, not the paper. I've seen whole strips of paint just peel right off the wall and wrap around the roller because of drywall dust. You have to use a PVA primer to seal the porous mud first, otherwise the finish coat flashes and looks completely dead and uneven in the spots where the joints are. 

But... yeah. I could be dealing with all that, stressing over whether the red is bleeding through the primer, and if I catch my reflection in a glossy door frame I just painted... the job doesn't matter anymore. All the technical stuff just drops out of my head, and it's straight back to stressing over my stomach.
